messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur had managed the Grand Sterling Hotel for twenty-two years, a tenure built on a foundation of unflappable calm and an innate sense of control. At sixty-seven, he moved with a practiced authority that reassured both staff and guests. That authority vanished four months ago in the hotel's back alley, on a cold Tuesday night. He was locking up when two men emerged from the shadows by the dumpsters. The reek of cheap whiskey hit him first, thick and cloying. Then came a guttural shout that echoed between the brick walls, and before he could react, he was slammed against the building, the rough surface scraping his cheek. They took his wallet and his watch, but what he remembered most was the feeling of utter powerlessness as they shoved him to the ground, laughing, before disappearing into the night.

The incident left more than bruises; it shattered a lifetime of assumptions. In the weeks that followed, Arthur had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, a truth he had simply been lucky enough to avoid until now. He felt a deep, abiding shame, a sense of being permanently humiliated by his inability to defend himself. This new certainty that people couldn't be trusted became the lens through which he saw everyone, from the guests checking in at the front desk to strangers on the street.

Because he was now certain that danger lurked everywhere and that people were inherently untrustworthy, Arthur felt he had no choice but to remain constantly on guard. This belief system fueled a state of relentless watchfulness. At home, a place that once felt like a sanctuary, he found himself checking the locks multiple times before bed, feeling on guard even in his own living room. His wife, Maria, learned not to touch his shoulder to get his attention; his reaction was so sharp, so alarmed, it was as if she had burned him. At work, he was no longer a calm presence but a coiled spring, his eyes constantly scanning the lobby, assessing every individual for potential threat.

This state of being perpetually superalert meant his nervous system was primed for attack. His hypervigilance actively scanned the environment for anything that resembled the mugging, transforming neutral events into potent threats. Now, a loud noise from the hotel kitchen wasn't just a dropped tray; it was the shout from the alley, an immediate danger that sent a jolt of ice through his veins. The scent of alcohol on a guest checking in was no longer just an observation but a visceral warning sign that made him want to back away. And his constant watchfulness meant that anyone who lingered too long near the elevators or seemed out of place was immediately flagged as 'acting suspiciously,' a potential predator in waiting.

His world, once expansive and manageable, began to shrink. He delegated the final lock-up duties, unable to bring himself to walk through the back alley. He became short-tempered with his staff, misinterpreting their casual conversations as carelessness that could invite danger. The job he once loved, a place of order and hospitality, now felt like a battlefield he had to survey every single day. The exhaustion was profound. Maria told him he seemed like a ghost in their home, present in body but absent in spirit, lost in a state of constant, silent alarm. It was after he accused a tourist of following him through the hotel lobby, causing a scene that required the intervention of his assistant manager, that he finally acknowledged the depth of his struggle. He sought therapy not just to escape the fear, but to reclaim the man he was before the alley—the man who believed in the good of people and felt safe in his own skin. What he feared most was that the humiliation had changed him permanently, that the watchful, frightened man he had become was all that was left.
